L0@P0: SI
L1@P0: A concise summary of the
L2@P0: International System of Units, SI
L3@P0: Metrology is the science of measurement and its application. Metrology includes
L4@P0: all theoretical and practical aspects of measurement, whatever the measurement
L5@P0: uncertainty and field of application.
L6@P0: The International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) was established by Article 1 of the Metre Convention, which was
L7@P0: signed on 20 May 1875. It is charged with providing the basis for a single, coherent system of measurements to be used
L8@P0: throughout the world and it operates under the authority of the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM).
L9@P0: The decimal metric system, dating from the time of the French Revolution, was based in 1799 on the metre and the kilogram.
L10@P0: Under the terms of the Metre Convention, new international prototypes of the metre and kilogram were manufactured and
L11@P0: formally adopted by the first General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in 1889. In 1960 the 11th CGPM
L12@P0: formally defined and established the International System of Units (SI). Since then the SI has been periodically updated to take
L13@P0: account of advances in science and the need for measurements in new domains. The last major revision was adopted by the
L14@P0: 26th CGPM (2018), which decided that the SI would be based on the fixed numerical values of a set of seven defining
L15@P0: constants from which the definitions of the seven base units of the SI would be deduced. This document is a summary of the
L16@P0: SI Brochure, a publication produced by the BIPM, which gives a detailed explanation of the current status of the SI.
L17@P0: The SI is the system of units in which:
L18@P0: • the unperturbed ground state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium 133 atom, ∆νCs, is 9 192 631 770 Hz,
L19@P0: • the speed of light in vacuum, c, is 299 792 458 m/s,
L20@P0: • the Planck constant, h, is 6.626 070 15 × 10−34 J s,
L21@P0: • the elementary charge, e, is 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 C,
L22@P0: • the Boltzmann constant, k, is 1.380 649 × 10−23 J/K,
L23@P0: • the Avogadro constant, NA, is 6.022 140 76 × 1023 mol−1,
L24@P0: • the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 1012 Hz, Kcd, is 683 lm/W,
L25@P0: where the hertz, joule, coulomb, lumen, and watt, with unit symbols Hz, J, C, lm, and W, respectively, are related to the units
L26@P0: second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, and candela, with unit symbols s, m, kg, A, K, mol, and cd, respectively,
L27@P0: according to Hz = s–1, J = kg m2
L28@P0:  s–2, C = A s, lm = cd sr, and W = kg m2 s–3.
L29@P0: These definitions specify the exact numerical value of each constant when its value is expressed in the corresponding SI unit.
L30@P0: By fixing the exact numerical value, the unit becomes defined, since the product of the numerical value and the unit has to
L31@P0: equal the value of the constant, which is invariant.
L32@P0: The defining constants have been chosen such that, when taken together, their units cover all of the units of the SI. In general,
L33@P0: there is no one-to-one correspondence between the defining constants and the SI base units, except for the caesium frequency
L34@P0: ∆νCs and the Avogadro constant NA. Any SI unit is a product of powers of these seven constants and a dimensionless factor.
L35@P0: For example: using Hz = s−1, one metre can be derived from the speed of light c and caesium frequency ∆νCs,

L51@P0: The concept of base units and derived units was used to define the SI until 2018. These categories, although no longer essential
L52@P0: in the SI, are maintained in view of their convenience and widespread use. The definitions of the base units, which follow from
L53@P0-1: the definition of the SI in terms of the seven defining constants, are given in Table 1.Table 1 The seven base units of the SI
L54@P1: Quantity SI unit
L55@P1: time The second, symbol s, is the SI unit of time. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the
L56@P1: caesium frequency, ∆νCs, the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the
L57@P1: caesium 133 atom, to be 9 192 631 770 when expressed in the unit Hz, which is equal to s−1.
L58@P1: length The metre, symbol m, is the SI unit of length. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of
L59@P1: the speed of light in vacuum, c, to be 299 792 458 when expressed in the unit m s−1, where the
L60@P1: second is defined in terms of ∆νCs.
L61@P1: mass The kilogram, symbol kg, is the SI unit of mass. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value
L62@P1: of the Planck constant, h, to be 6.626 070 15 ×10−34 when expressed in the unit J s, which is equal
L63@P1: to kg m2
L64@P1:  s−1, where the metre and the second are defined in terms of c and ∆νCs.
L65@P1: electric current The ampere, symbol A, is the SI unit of electric current. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical
L66@P1: value of the elementary charge, e, to be 1.602 176 634 ×10−19 when expressed in the unit C, which
L67@P1: is equal to A s, where the second is defined in terms of ∆νCs.
L68@P1: thermodynamic
L69@P1: temperature
L70@P1: The kelvin, symbol K, is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. It is defined by taking the fixed
L71@P1: numerical value of the Boltzmann constant, k, to be 1.380 649 ×10−23 when expressed in the unit
L72@P1: J K−1, which is equal to kg m2 s−2 K−1, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of
L73@P1: h, c and ∆νCs.
L74@P1: amount of substance The mole, symbol mol, is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly
L75@P1: 6.022 140 76 × 1023 elementary entities. This number is the fixed numerical value of the Avogadro
L76@P1: constant, NA, when expressed in the unit mol−1 and is called the Avogadro number.
L77@P1: The amount of substance, symbol n, of a system is a measure of the number of specified elementary
L78@P1: entities. An elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or
L79@P1: specified group of particles.
L80@P1: luminous intensity The candela, symbol cd, is the SI unit of luminous intensity in a given direction. It is defined by
L81@P1: taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency
L82@P1: 540 × 1012 Hz, Kcd, to be 683 when expressed in the unit lm W−1, which is equal to
L83@P1: cd sr W−1, or cd sr kg−1 m−2 s3, where the kilogram, metre and second are defined in terms of h, c
L84@P1: and ∆νCs.
L85@P1: All other quantities may be called “derived quantities” and are expressed using derived units, which can be written as products
L86@P1: of powers of base units. Twenty-two derived units are given a special name, as listed in Table 2.
L87@P1: Table 2 Derived units with special names in the SI

L99@P1: electric resistance ohm Ω V/A = kg m2 s−3 A−2
L100@P1: electric conductance siemens S A/V = kg−1 m−2 s3 A2

L102@P1: magnetic flux density tesla T Wb/m2 = kg s−2 A−1

L107@P1: activity referred to a radionuclide becquerel Bq s−1
L108@P1: absorbed dose, kerma gray Gy J/kg = m2 s−2

L110@P1-2: catalytic activity katal kat mol s−1Although the hertz and the becquerel are both equal to the reciprocal second, hertz is used only for periodic phenomena, and
L111@P2: becquerel is used only for stochastic processes in radioactive decay.
L112@P2: The unit of Celsius temperature is the degree Celsius, °C, which is equal in magnitude to the kelvin, K, the unit of
L113@P2: thermodynamic temperature. The quantity Celsius temperature t is related to thermodynamic temperature T by the equation
L114@P2: t/°C = T/K − 273.15.
L115@P2: The sievert is also used for the quantities ‘directional dose equivalent’ and ‘personal dose equivalent’.
L116@P2: There are many more quantities than units. For each quantity, there is only one SI unit (although this may often be expressed in
L117@P2: different ways by using the special names), while the same SI unit may be used to express the values of several different
L118@P2: quantities (for example, the SI unit J/K may be used to express the value of both heat capacity and entropy). It is therefore
L119@P2: important not to use the unit alone to specify the quantity. This applies both to scientific texts and also to measuring
L120@P2: instruments (i.e. an instrument read-out should indicate both the quantity concerned and the unit).
L121@P2: There are quantities with the unit one, symbol 1, that are ratios of two quantities of the same kind. For example, refractive
L122@P2: index is the ratio of two speeds, and relative permittivity is the ratio of the permittivity of a dielectric medium to that of free
L123@P2: space. There are also quantities that are a number of entities, for example, the number of cellular or biomolecular entities.
L124@P2: These quantities also have the unit one. The unit one is the neutral element of any system of units. Quantities with the unit one
L125@P2: can therefore be considered as traceable to the SI. However, when expressing the values of quantities with the unit one, the unit
L126@P2: symbol 1 is not written.
L127@P2: Decimal multiples and sub-multiples of SI units
L128@P2: A set of prefixes have been adopted for use with the SI units in order to express the values of quantities that are either much
L129@P2: larger than, or much smaller than, the SI unit when used without any prefix. They can be used with any SI unit. The SI prefixes
L130@P2: are listed in Table 3.
L131@P2: Table 3 The SI prefixes
L132@P2: Factor Name Symbol Factor Name Symbol
L133@P2: 101 deca da 10−1 deci d
L134@P2: 102 hecto h 10−2 centi c
L135@P2: 103 kilo k 10−3 milli m
L136@P2: 106 mega M 10−6 micro µ
L137@P2: 109 giga G 10−9 nano n
L138@P2: 1012 tera T 10−12 pico p
L139@P2: 1015 peta P 10−15 femto f
L140@P2: 1018 exa E 10−18 atto a
L141@P2: 1021 zetta Z 10−21 zepto z
L142@P2: 1024 yotta Y 10−24 yocto y
L143@P2: 1027 ronna R 10−27 ronto r
L144@P2: 1030 quetta Q 10−30 quecto q
L145@P2: When the prefixes are used, the prefix name and the unit name are combined to form a single word. Similarly, the prefix
L146@P2: symbol and the unit symbol are written without any space to form a single symbol, which may itself be raised to any power.
L147@P2: For example, we may write: kilometre, km; microvolt, µV; or femtosecond, fs.
L148@P2: When the SI units are used without any prefixes, the resulting set of units is described as being coherent in the following
L149@P2: sense: when only coherent units are used, equations between the numerical values of quantities take exactly the same form as
L150@P2: the equations between the quantities themselves. The use of a coherent set of units has technical advantages, for example in
L151@P2: quantity calculus (see the SI Brochure).
L152@P2: The kilogram, kg, is problematic because the name already includes a prefix, for historical reasons. Multiples and
L153@P2: sub-multiples of the kilogram are written by combining prefixes with the gram: thus we write milligram, mg,
L154@P2: not microkilogram, µkg.
L155@P2: Units outside the SI
L156@P2: The SI is the only system of units that is universally recognized, so it has a distinct advantage for establishing international
L157@P2: dialogue. The use of the SI, as a standard system of units, simplifies the teaching of science. For these reasons, the use of
L158@P2: SI units is recommended in all fields of science and technology. Other units, i.e. non-SI units, are generally defined in terms of
L159@P2-3: SI units using conversion factors. Nonetheless, some non-SI units are still widely used. A few, such as the minute, hour and day as units of time, will always be
L160@P3: used because they are part of our culture. Others are used for historical reasons, to meet the needs of special interest groups, or
L161@P3: because there is no convenient SI alternative. It will always remain the prerogative of a scientist to use the units that are
L162@P3: considered to be best suited to the purpose. However, when non-SI units are used, the correspondence to the SI should always
L163@P3: be quoted. A selection of non-SI units is listed in Table 4 with their conversion factors to the SI. For a more comprehensive
L164@P3: list, see the SI Brochure.
L165@P3: Table 4 A selection of non-SI units
L166@P3: The symbol for the litre is an exception to the general rule that the first letter of a unit symbol is only a capital when the unit is
L167@P3: named after a person; either a lower case letter ‘l’ or a capital ‘L’ may be used, the capital is allowed in this case to avoid
L168@P3: confusion between the lower case letter l and the number one, 1.
L169@P3: The language of science: using the SI to express the values of quantities
L170@P3: The value of a quantity is written as the product of a number and a unit. The number multiplying the unit is the numerical value
L171@P3: of the quantity in that unit. A single space is always left between the number and the unit. The numerical value depends on the
L172@P3: choice of unit, so that the same value of a quantity may have different numerical values when expressed in different units, as in
L173@P3: the examples provided below.
L174@P3: The speed of a bicycle is approximately
L175@P3: v = 5.0 m/s = 18 km/h.
L176@P3: The wavelength of one of the yellow lines of the sodium doublet is
L177@P3: λ = 5.896 × 10−7 m = 589.6 nm.
L178@P3: Quantity symbols are written using italic (slanting) type, and they are generally single letters of the Latin or Greek alphabet.
L179@P3: Either capital or lower case letters may be used, and additional information on the quantity may be added as a subscript or as
L180@P3: information in parentheses.
L181@P3: Authorities such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and international scientific unions such as the
L182@P3: International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP) and the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry
L183@P3: (IUPAC) have specified recommended symbols for many quantities. Examples include:
L184@P3: T for thermodynamic temperature
L185@P3: Cp for heat capacity at constant pressure
L186@P3: xi for the mole fraction (amount fraction) of species i
L187@P3: µr for relative permeability.
L188@P3: Unit symbols are written using roman (upright) type, regardless of the type used in the surrounding text. They are
L189@P3: mathematical entities and not abbreviations; unit symbols are never followed by a full stop (except at the end of a sentence) nor
L190@P3: by an ‘s’ for the plural. The use of the correct form for unit symbols is mandatory, and is illustrated by examples in the SI
L191@P3: Brochure. Unit symbols may be more than a single letter. They are written in lower case letters (for example: metre, m; second,
L192@P3: s; or mole, mol), the exception being that the first letter is a capital when the unit is named after a person (for example: ampere,
L193@P3: A; kelvin, K; hertz, Hz; or coulomb, C). However, when the name of a unit is spelled in full, it should begin with a lower case
L194@P3: letter (except at the beginning of a sentence), to distinguish the unit from the person (for example, the name kelvin for the unit
L195@P3: of thermodynamic temperature is derived from the proper name Kelvin).
L196@P3: When writing the value of a quantity as the product of a numerical value and a unit, both the number and the unit may be
L197@P3: treated by the ordinary rules of algebra. For example, the equation T = 293 K may equally be written as T/K = 293.
L198@P3: This procedure is described as the use of quantity calculus, or the algebra of quantities. It is often useful to use the ratio of a
L199@P3: quantity to its unit as the heading for columns in a table, or for labelling the axes of a graph, so that the entries in the table or
L200@P3: the labels for the tick marks on the axes are all simply denoted by numbers. The example (Table 5) shows a table of the
L201@P3: velocity squared versus pressure, with the columns labelled in this way.
L202@P3: Quantity Unit Symbol Relation to SI
L203@P3: time minute min 1 min = 60 s
L204@P3: time hour h 1 h = 3600 s
L205@P3: time day d 1 d = 86 400 s
L206@P3: volume litre L or l 1 L = 1 dm3
L207@P3: mass tonne t 1 t = 1000 kg
L208@P3-4: energy electronvolt eV 1 eV = 1.602 176 634 × 10−19 J Table 5 Example of column heading in a table of the velocity squared versus pressure
L209@P4: p/kPa ν2/(m/s)2
L210@P4: 48.73 94 766
L211@P4: 72.87 94 771
L212@P4: 135.42 94 784
L213@P4: In forming products or quotients of unit symbols the normal rules of algebra apply. In forming products of unit symbols, a
L214@P4: space should be left between units (or alternatively a half-high centred dot can be used as a multiplication symbol).
L215@P4: The importance of the space should be noted: the product of a metre and a second is denoted by m s (with a space), but ms
L216@P4: (without a space) is used to denote a millisecond. In addition, when forming complicated products of units, brackets or
L217@P4: negative exponents should be used to avoid ambiguities. For example, the molar gas constant R is given by:
L218@P4: pVm/T = R = 8.314 Pa m3 mol−1 K−1
L219@P4:  = 8.314 Pa m3/(mol K).
L220@P4: When formatting numbers, the decimal marker may be either a point (i.e. a full stop) or a comma, depending on the
L221@P4: circumstances. For documents in the English language a point is usual, but for many languages and in many countries a comma
L222@P4: is usual.
L223@P4: When a number has many digits, it is customary to group the digits into threes about the decimal point to aid readability.
L224@P4: This is not essential, but it is often done and is generally helpful. When this format is used, the groups of three digits should be
L225@P4: separated only by a space. Neither dots nor commas are ever inserted in the spaces between groups.
L226@P4: The uncertainty in the numerical value of a quantity may often be conveniently shown by giving the uncertainty in the least
L227@P4: significant digits in parentheses after the number.
L228@P4: For example: The value of the electron mass is given in the 2014 CODATA listing of fundamental constants as
L229@P4:  me = 9.109 383 56 (11) × 10−31 kg,
L230@P4: where 11 is the standard uncertainty in the final digits quoted for the numerical value.
L231@P4: For further information, see the BIPM website, or the SI Brochure 9th edition, which is available at
L232@P4: www.bipm.org
